headlines.title: 'A new Plaza Accord?' Japan's battle against yen bears enters new phase

ripple_effect.name: Major coordinated or sustained move in the US dollar

historical_precedents.what_happened: Finance ministers from France, West Germany, Japan, the UK, and the US agreed at New York's Plaza Hotel to jointly intervene in currency markets to depreciate the US dollar, which had strengthened roughly 50% against major currencies between 1980 and 1985.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The dollar fell about 4% against other major currencies the Monday after the agreement was made public, and continued weakening over the following two years — a decline substantial enough that the G5/G7 later signed the 1987 Louvre Accord to halt it.

historical_precedents.event: US Dollar Index reaches a multi-decade high
historical_precedents.what_happened: A combination of aggressive Fed rate hikes, the war in Ukraine, and a resulting European energy crisis drove the US Dollar Index sharply higher through 2022.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The index closed 2022 at 110.05, its highest level since the early 1980s (it had peaked around 151.47 in 1984), squeezing countries and companies with dollar-denominated debt and import bills.

possibility_chains: A sharply stronger dollar has historically made dollar-denominated debt more expensive to service for foreign governments and companies that earn revenue in other currencies, raising default risk in the most exposed economies.
A strong dollar has historically weighed on the earnings of large US multinational companies, since revenue earned abroad translates back into fewer dollars.

Coordinated multi-country currency interventions, as in the Plaza Accord, have historically shown that large, sustained dollar moves can be at least partly reversed by deliberate policy action when major economies agree to act together — though such coordination has been rare.

headlines.title: At Beijing AI-themed bar, DeepSeek tokens come with the pints - Reuters

ripple_effect.name: Open-source AI model release and market disruption

historical_precedents.event: DeepSeek's R1 model release triggers a historic Nvidia stock selloff
historical_precedents.what_happened: Chinese AI startup DeepSeek released its open-weight R1 reasoning model on January 20, 2025, claiming competitive performance with leading US models at a fraction of the reported training cost; by January 27, 2025 its free app had become the most-downloaded app on the US iOS App Store, overtaking ChatGPT, as investors began questioning whether the scale of capital spending underpinning US AI infrastructure was justified.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Nvidia's shares fell roughly 17-18% on January 27, 2025, wiping out about $600 billion in market capitalization in a single session - described as the largest single-company market-capitalization loss in US stock market history - as the announcement rattled the broader AI-infrastructure trade.

possibility_chains: A cheaper or open-weight AI model that matches proprietary competitors' performance has historically prompted investors to question the return on massive infrastructure capital spending by the incumbent leaders, even before any actual revenue impact materializes.

Open-weight model releases have historically lowered the cost of entry for smaller companies and researchers to build AI applications, broadening competition beyond the handful of firms that can afford to train frontier models from scratch.

A single dramatic repricing event in AI-related stocks has historically been followed by continued underlying capital investment in AI infrastructure, suggesting markets and long-term corporate strategy can diverge sharply in the short term.
